listenings.text: Right, so you have three options here. This one is the newest and it is the fastest board in the shop, no question. It is also the hardest one to surf and it has the least volume, so on a small day you are going to hate it. This second one is secondhand, it is only two years old, and it is half the price. Honestly, it is better value than anything else on this wall. And the third one is the most expensive board we have. It is the best board in the shop, I am not going to pretend otherwise, but for six months? It is not worth it, mate. Buy the secondhand one and spend the rest on the bus.

Okay, two options. The town beach is closer, it is ten minutes on foot, and that is the only good thing about it, because it is the most crowded beach on this whole coast. The other one is forty minutes on the bus. The waves there are much better and it is a lot emptier, so yes, the trip is worth it. One warning though. It is a reef, not a beach break. On a small day it is the best wave around here. On a big day it is more dangerous than anything you have surfed at home, so go with somebody the first time.

reading.rtitle: Your first board in Australia: a short buyer's guide
paras: The first question is not which board is the best. It is which board is the best FOR YOU, at the spot where you are actually going to surf.

A shortboard is faster and it turns better, but it is much harder to learn on, because it has less volume and it floats less. A longboard is slower and bigger, but on a small day it is easier and you catch three times more waves. If your local spot is a small beach break, the longboard is the better choice, even if the shortboard looks cooler.

New or secondhand? A new board is better, of course. It is also two or three times more expensive. A secondhand board that is one or two years old is usually in good condition, and it is the cheapest way to get in the water. For a six month stay it is almost always worth it.

One last thing, and it is the most important one. Ask where the waves break. Sand is forgiving; a reef is not. A beach break is safer for your first weeks, and the fins on your board are cheaper to replace than your knee.
